title: Advice for those developing games with AI, so they don't make the same mistake I did.
author: Elegant_Ad4923
selftext: For a while now, I've been developing a web-based RTS game, a dream of mine. At first, it was great; I was hyped and felt like Hulk, capable of doing anything. After happily spending my tokens for a while, the first problems started to appear. Because I didn't clearly define the scope from the beginning, I acted on the assumption that I would correct it later, and that was the worst decision. After a while, the development process progressed by opening many branches and constantly adding new things and making patches. This process negatively affected me both mentally and in terms of discouraging me. As I neared the end, I remember feeling relieved, thinking, "Finally, it's over." Not because I had completed it, but because I was free. I'm writing this so that you don't experience the same thing; please, please define your scope, goals, and plan well before you start. This will help you be more disciplined and... This will prevent your guidance system from being disrupted in the future. I wish you all the best in your work, I just wanted to vent 😅

replies.author: craigitsfriday
replies.body:
This is true. You are always the worst judge of your own work. The fix is playtesting often with fresh eyes. Alot of this thread is talking about game design and game production. These are two different skills than game engineering, which as ai devs we are passing the workload to the LLM.

It's true that a well defined project plan (GDD and TDD) can help you keep your larger projects on the rails, but a word of caution to new devs, you are creating a waterfall project which has largely been dropped from traditional game dev due to the pitfalls that it brings. Waterfall can easily fall apart when major shifts are required. Agile has been king for decades to replace this. My advice is to keep your scope small and build bottom up, playtesting often before taking on a big project. This issue is the equivalent of a new dev aiming for their dream MMO on the first shot. You need to cut your teeth on smaller managed projects to learn and grow. I definitely recommend picking up some books on game design and game production of you are new to field. Best of luck on your projects.

comments.author: Novaworld7
comments.body:
I'm going at it all solo as well for an MMORPG (like everyone else I suppose, delusional I know). 

What i did and it's helped tremendously is I started with a TDD and a GDD roughly at the same time. 

The GDD started with my vision and then I used some internal skills for it to ask me about 50-100 questions around the design to better understand it. Now all of this is tracked via MD files in a folder also synced to GH. 

That started the foundation of the full scope. From there I went back to the TDD and did the same thing to understand hardware requirements / deployment needs / stress test / realistic expectations. 

Then I started building in a phased way and very quickly it sprawled out into this massive war on many fronts because systems are very tightly coupled. Despite this I chose 1 system at a time foundationally and worked on them upwards. For example, Stats / skills / spells / items are all needed for formula making, but if you try to build them all together you'll struggle. So I just worked from simplest to most complex. 

I source place holder assets on fab, and I am focused on establishing systems / polish as swapping out models / VFX / SFX is much easier when templates are in place. 

I'll close with I also set up specific skills to spawn my fleet of agents and they can spawn agents, they all work together to update documents keep me honest about decisions, and I have a QA doc and a questions doc. Everything gets logged and they surface contradictions etc. 

All of this combined has helped me dramatically manage burn out / stay focused and not scope creep. 

Sorry for the monologue, stay savage and keep trucking baby.

replies.author: EmergencyShutdown
replies.body:
Multiple agents working together is a game changer. 

Set up a dedicated project manager - tell them to outline what repositories need to exist and establish the ground rules. Each other agent gets a defined expertise -  and I've found the pairing or stacking two agents also really helps prevent issues.  For example - create an art director role separate from the artist or asset creation role.  The art director can force the artist to iterate and prevent them from getting lazy or taking shortcuts.  Keep a role in place for a dedicated gameplay consultant that makes sure the actual engineering team is prioritizing and not getting stuck in the weeds.  

You can also really optimize models this way - keep your high level planners using flagship models, while using the tier down to implement and test. 

Your only interface becomes the project manager - who tells you what you need to test and sign off on, and to verify that it's going as planned. 

And if you weren't aware - agents can communicate between sessions easily - even different products - Claude and codex will happily set up inboxes and message back and forth, setting up an automatic message checking routine.

replies.author: aeturnis-dev
replies.body:
I operate this way as well and another invaluable thing at your disposal is prior art research. Have your agent do a deep dive on a mechanic you are thinking about. Researching will save you a lot of pain if reinventing something that sort of works versus something that does work that you can use or adopt.

For example I wanted animated 3D cloth, but I can’t model and Claude Code doesn’t have eyes, but it can research and math like a son of a bitch. And I don’t limit the research to a specific field. 

For headless cloth animation of 3D via script, cross domain research helped tremendously in creating a cloth simulation by incorporating the behavior of springs. That’s not cloth, but for the cloth simulation the math worked really well.

I’ve also found that math and tests and simulations are paramount to helping guide your agent to do what you want, and I’m terrible at math, not a programmer or game designer. I just ask “What if?” A lot. 

Don’t be afraid to throw math and whimsical “What ifs?” At a problem you come across.

And please give yourself milestones or definitions “of done” for a feature or something, or you’ll always dig deeper and deeper until you can’t get out of the hole.

replies.author: Novaworld7
replies.body:
Simplest way I have found is to find a program that you can speak to. I have uses chatgpt a few times to save my Claude tokens. But a tool like monologue works as well and windows key + H if you are feeling dicy. 

Once you have a way to speech to text, then just rant your idea. Once that's been completed for part 1, and you have it in a text or MD file. Then feed that mangled thing to a model and tell it to shape it into a GDD and flag what's missing in a GDD follow up document. I prefer md because I tell it to group it into a table, and ask one question per row. 

Then I tell it to review the GDD and ask gap questions and to adversarially review the systems and call me out on shortcomings. I don't need a yes man, I need a colleague whose going to hit me with what I need to hear, I don't need a cheerleader. 

Then I keep going with that and reviewing the systems myself till I feel it's complete enough to make an MVP. Once the MVP is locked anything else is scope creep + noise. It'll come in later if I approve it as a patch. 

Once the GDD is complete I tell it to ask me all the questions needed to make a TDD, we need to think about hosting, protection, number of players, relevancy, etc. 

Then it's time to get to work and I test in phases with QA docs that has a master, a folder per day, QA logs per QA session a master QA that stores each pass / fail / and a decision document that tracks date + reason + system as to whatever it is.

comments.author: Furyan9x
comments.body:
I had scope creep before I even opened Unity for the first time lol but the way I planned it out with Claude is a way that lets me start very small with very achievable goals, and just link together a bunch of those to eventually have something massive. 

We classified each section of my GDD as Foundation, Basics, Expansion, Complexity, Luxury, Wishful. Then wrote an implementation plan with all systems/features listed in order of importance so that nothing is built before something else it requires. 

So, I laid the foundations for everything first, and now I'm working on basics. Then each system/feature gets its expansion, then I'll add the complexity layer, and finally, luxury. Luxury is mostly reserved for art work, models, S/VFX, Animations, Voice Acting, cut scenes, etc. 

My game will be fully functional without the luxury items (it will have those things, but they may not be high quality) but the experience would be much more... Luxurious.. with high quality assets. 

Wishful is reserved for things that most likely won't make it into the game, but fortunately I only have one thing there at the moment: the ability to support all players on one mega server. 

I had to upgrade to the Claude Max because I hit my weekly limit in 3 days. We'll see if it's financially viable to keep the sub or drop down to 2 Pro subs.

replies.author: Elegant_Ad4923
replies.body:
Yeah, I think the project getting too big was the main problem. As I kept adding features, I started losing track of how some parts of the code were connected.

Switching between different models made things worse sometimes. At one point I had to continue development in Antigravity, and I almost ended up breaking the entire project. It took quite a bit of work to get things back on track.

I think my biggest mistake was not documenting the project structure properly from the beginning. Even with a good model, things can get messy when the project grows and you keep switching tools.

Before starting development, make a game bible and well defined ideas, what is happening here is called scope creep, and it's not about AI itself, it happened with manual coding as well.
